Once a ball is on the three-slot platform, its chance of eventually being ejected (and thus winning) depends only on how many balls remain in the system and which slot it occupies.

Last three balls on the platform (nos. 98, 99, 100):
• #100 starts in slot 3, with no balls left on the ramp.  
 If piston 3 fires it is ejected immediately.  
 If piston 2 fires, balls 98 (slot 1) and 99 (slot 2) leave, leaving #100 alone; it must eventually be hit by piston 1.  
 If piston 1 fires, ball 98 leaves; #100 shifts forward and again must eventually be hit by its piston.  
In every case #100 is certain to be ejected, so its probability of winning is 1.

Ball 99’s winning probability is lower (5⁄6), and all earlier balls are still lower (17⁄27 or less).  Therefore the unique best pick is ball 100.
A ball can leave the machine in two ways: (1) it is struck by the piston that lines up with its position (ejected) or (2) it sits in the first slot when either the second-slot or third-slot piston fires, in which case it merely rolls away (released).  

Any ball that has another ball queued behind it can end up in the first slot while a different piston fires, so it always carries some chance of being released instead of ejected.  

The very last ball on the ramp (ball 100) is different.  Once it reaches the platform there are no balls behind it, so if it ever sits in the first slot the second- and third-slot pistons cannot eject anything and therefore cannot trigger the “roll away” release.  Consequently ball 100 must eventually leave only by being struck by its own piston; it is guaranteed to be ejected.  

Because every other ball has a non-zero chance of being released, ball 100 has the highest (indeed, 100%) probability of being ejected.

Let the three hidden amounts, in non-decreasing order, be a ≤ b ≤ c with a + b + c = 30.

Constraints
1.  One box has at least 2 coins (trivially satisfied when the total is 30).
2.  Some pair differs by exactly 6, so one of the equalities a = b − 6, b = c − 6, or a = c − 6 holds.

Minimal possible largest box
•  If b = a + 6:  c = 24 − 2a, and ordering forces a ≤ 6 ⇒ c ≥ 12.
•  If c = b + 6:  a = 24 − 2b, with 8 ≤ b ≤ 12 ⇒ c ≥ 14.
•  If c = a + 6:  6 ≤ a ≤ 8 ⇒ c ≥ 12.
So in every legal distribution the largest box holds at least 12 coins, and 12 is attainable (e.g. 6,12,12).

Bob’s guess pattern and host’s reply
Bob submits three guesses g1 ≤ g2 ≤ g3.  The host then pairs g3 with a, g2 with b, and g1 with c (this minimises Bob’s take).  Bob receives gi only if gi ≤ corresponding coins.

To guarantee anything from the c-box we must have g1 ≤ 12 (12 is the least c can ever be).  Any amount above 12 can be defeated by the distribution 6,12,12 (yielding zero from that box).

The smallest possible middle amount b is 6 (e.g. 0,6,24). If g2 > 6 the host can choose that distribution and give Bob nothing from the b-box.  Hence no second guess bigger than 6 can be protected while keeping g1 ≥ g2.

Therefore the best Bob can do is to put all his betting power into one protected guess: choose (12,12,12).  Against any legal distribution:
•  At least one box contains ≥12 coins, so Bob gets at least one payoff of 12.
•  The host can make at most one box hold ≥12 while the others hold <12 (e.g. 4,10,16), limiting Bob’s total to exactly 12.

Thus Bob’s optimal guaranteed haul is 12 coins, each worth $1,000.
The host can arrange the 30 coins as three non-negative integers (a,b,c) that sum to 30, such that some pair differs by exactly 6.  

For any fixed guess r made for every box, Bob is guaranteed r·N coins, where N is the minimum possible number of boxes that can still hold at least r coins in every legal distribution.  

1.  If r>12 the host can choose the distribution 12,12,6, in which no box reaches r, so Bob could get 0.  Hence r must be ≤12.
2.  Take r=12.  Whatever the distribution is, at least one box must contain 12 or more coins (the maximal coin count cannot be below 12, otherwise the total would be <30 while satisfying the 6-coin difference).  The host can, however, arrange a distribution such as 15,9,6 (15−9=6) in which exactly one box meets or exceeds 12, so Bob will get exactly 12 coins.  
3.  For any r<12 the host can arrange a distribution with only one box ≥r (e.g. 16,8,6 for r between 8 and 10, or 24,6,0 for r=6).  Thus Bob’s guaranteed take is at most r<12 in these cases.

Therefore r=12 maximises the minimum number of coins Bob can force, giving a guarantee of 12 coins.  Each coin is worth $1 000, so the minimum amount of money Bob can be sure to win is 12 000.
